setupSteps: Check the machine and its mode. If it is a combined leg press / hack squat frame, confirm it is in hack squat mode (the release and the foot platform differ by model; read the label or ask staff).

Look at the safety system. Find the safety release (usually rotating side handles, or a lever) and the safety stops (pins or bars that catch the sled at a set height). On many designs the handles are turned from a front-facing position to a diagonal one to free the sled (Bodybuilding.com; model differences apply). The exact method Not found as a general rule.

Plates. Start with the empty sled (find the sled's own weight on the label if shown, otherwise Not found) or one light plate per side. Load both sides evenly, push each plate fully onto the horn and fit collars or the horn clip if provided.
Set the safety stops at a height just below your planned lowest point, so the sled cannot go deeper than you can recover from (RitFit; Powerlifting Technique advises setting stops before each set).
Step in and stand with your back flat against the back pad, with your hips and upper back against it, head relaxed and eyes forward.

Adjust the shoulder pads (usually a pin or a lever) so the pads rest firmly on top of your shoulders without pinching your neck or lifting your shoulders up. If the pads are too high, your shoulders get squeezed up; too low, you cannot stand tall. Note the setting for next time.

Place the feet on the platform about shoulder-width apart, in the middle of the platform, toes turned out slightly (about 10–30°, est.). Healthline and most guides use shoulder width; StrengthLog notes toe angle and width made little difference in the studies it cites.

Height on the platform. Feet lower on the platform shift work toward the quads and calves; higher feet shift work toward the glutes and hamstrings (StrengthLog; bodybuilding guides). The one controlled study found (Escamilla 2001, on the leg press) no significant difference in quad activity between high and low foot positions, so this is a small effect. Beginners should keep the feet mid-platform: very low feet push the knees far forward and lift the heels, and very high feet may make the lower back leave the pad (guide advice).
Release the safety. Hold the side handles lightly, stand up to take the load, and turn the handles to release the sled (one hand at a time, only after you are set).

steps.title: Stand tall and brace
steps.action: With the sled released and your arms by your sides or lightly on the handles, press your back into the pad and gently tighten your stomach.
steps.feel: Back and hips firm against the pad; weight on the whole foot.
steps.visualCheck: Side: head, shoulders, hips in one line against the pad; knees soft, not locked. Front: feet shoulder-width, knees over the second toe.

steps.title: Start the descent
steps.action: Bend your knees and hips together and lower the sled slowly, pushing your knees out in line with your toes.
steps.feel: Front thighs and buttocks loading; heels pressed down.
steps.breathing: Keep breathing in as you lower.
steps.visualCheck: Side: shoulders stay under the pads and the back stays on the pad. Front: both knees move out over the toes, not inward.

steps.title: Reach a comfortable depth
steps.action: Lower until your thighs are about parallel to the platform (knees about 90–100° of bend), or only as deep as you keep your back on the pad and heels down.
steps.feel: Strong thigh stretch; no pinch in the front of the knee or the hips.
steps.breathing: Hold the breath only briefly if you need to brace, otherwise keep breathing steadily.
steps.visualCheck: Side: thighs about level with the platform; heels flat. Front: knees in line with toes, hips level.

steps.title: Press up
steps.action: Push the whole foot into the platform and straighten your knees and hips together.
steps.feel: Quads and glutes pushing; heels and mid-foot doing the work.
steps.visualCheck: Side: back stays on the pad; hips do not shoot up faster than the shoulders. Front: knees do not cave in.

steps.title: Stop just short of locking
steps.action: At the top, keep a small bend in the knees.
steps.feel: Weight held by the muscles, not the knee joints.
steps.visualCheck: Side: knees slightly bent, hips under the shoulders. Front: legs straight but soft.

steps.title: Repeat smoothly for the planned reps, without bouncing off the bottom
Finish and re-engage the safety
steps.action: After the last rep, press the sled to the top, turn the handles back to lock the sled, and then step out.
steps.feel: Legs tired, no sharp knee or back pain.
steps.visualCheck: The handles are back in the locked position (guides tell you to re-engage the release at the end of the set); plates are even on both sides.

commonMistakes.title: Knees caving inward
commonMistakes.text: Knees caving inward. Why: strains the knee, shows the load is too heavy or the hips are weak (guide advice). Fix: lower the weight, push the knees out over the toes.

commonMistakes.title: Heels lifting
commonMistakes.text: Heels lifting. Why: shifts the weight to the toes and pushes the knees forward. Fix: move the feet slightly higher on the platform and reduce depth until heels stay flat.

commonMistakes.title: Lower back leaving the pad at the bottom
commonMistakes.text: Lower back leaving the pad at the bottom. Why: rounds the spine under load. Fix: stop higher and keep the back on the pad (lower the range, lighter load).

commonMistakes.title: Locking the knees at the top
commonMistakes.text: Locking the knees at the top. Why: puts load on the joints, not the muscles. Fix: stop with a small bend.

commonMistakes.title: Dropping into the bottom and bouncing
commonMistakes.text: Dropping into the bottom and bouncing. Why: hits the safety stops, stresses the knees and is loud. Fix: 3 seconds down and a brief pause.

commonMistakes.title: Loading too much, too soon
commonMistakes.text: Loading too much, too soon. Why: Healthline lists too much weight as a mistake that stops you reaching proper depth. Fix: start with the empty sled; add plates only when 3 sets of 12 are smooth.

commonMistakes.title: Pulling on the handles to cheat
commonMistakes.text: Pulling on the handles to cheat. Why: shifts the work to the arms and shoulders. Fix: hold the handles lightly.

commonMistakes.title: Forgetting to re-engage the safety
commonMistakes.text: Forgetting to re-engage the safety. Why: the sled can move when you step out or when another member steps in. Fix: lock it after the last rep and before leaving the machine.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath on every rep
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath on every rep. Why: raises blood pressure (see Gym 10, MacDougall data). Fix: breathe out as you push up.

safetyNotes: Knee pain or kneecap pain (patellofemoral pain): kneecap load rises with depth, peaking near 90° of knee bend; reviews show most trials for kneecap pain excluded deep squats (PMC review). Use a shorter range, lighter weight, or choose the leg press. Stop if pain rises during or the day after.

Lower back problems: the back pad supports the spine, but do not let the back peel off the pad or the hips tuck under. Healthline suggests people with lower back or knee pain take care. Ask a clinician about depth and load.
Shoulder or neck problems: the pads rest on the shoulders and load goes through them. If the pads press on an injured area, choose the leg press (Gym 10).

High blood pressure / heart disease: breathe out on every push, no sets to failure, moderate loads. Do not lift if resting BP is 180/120 mmHg or higher; get clearance at 140–179/90–119 (secondary ACSM-aligned sources).

Pregnancy: the angled, back-supported hack squat is not a position that ACOG specifically addresses; reduce load, avoid breath-holding and ask your obstetrician (hack-squat-specific advice Not found).
Recent surgery: follow your surgeon's limits.
Larger bodies, tall or very short users: check the machine's maximum user weight, whether the shoulder pads fit, and whether you can reach the foot platform and release.
